text: Hands-on lab: build a complete test suite for a small quantum function — construction tests, a statevector check, and a statistical test — and organize them the way a real CI pipeline would run them.

This lesson covers structuring a tests directory mixing fast construction tests and slower statistical tests, using pytest markers to tier them by speed and cost, writing a complete test file for a non-trivial circuit, and a deliberately-introduced failing case to practice last lesson's debugging order.

This lab builds a full test suite for a three-qubit GHZ-state function that raises a value error below two qubits, applies a Hadamard, then a chain of CX gates, then measures everything. Registering custom pytest markers in pyproject.toml lets fast and slow tests be selected separately — construction tests run on every push in well under a second, while statistical tests run on a merge to main or a nightly job.

The construction tests, marked and parametrized across several qubit counts, check the gate sequence without ever executing the circuit. The statevector check, also marked as a fast construction-tier test even though it's conceptually the Lesson 8 debugging technique used proactively, confirms the exact GHZ state structure with zero sampling noise. These run first and fastest, and they're the ones most likely to catch a real logic bug.

The statistical test runs last, marked separately so it only runs on the slower tier. It runs the circuit on a seeded simulator, computes a z-score against the expected fifty-fifty split between the all-zeros and all-ones outcomes, and asserts it's within the ninety-nine percent confidence threshold. This is the one test that can occasionally fail by chance even on correct code, which is exactly why it carries an explicit, documented confidence threshold instead of an exact assertion.

Now suppose someone edits the loop to swap control and target, calling cx with the qubit indices reversed. Running the construction-tier tests first: the gate-sequence test still passes, because it only counts gate names, not which qubit is the control. But the statevector test fails immediately, because the resulting entangled state is structurally different. This is exactly last lesson's debugging order in action — the statevector check catches the logic bug before you'd ever need to run a single shot.

Before considering a quantum function's test coverage done, confirm: construction tests cover gate sequence, qubit count, and parameter wiring across multiple sizes; edge cases have explicit tests; a statevector test exists to catch logic bugs with zero sampling noise; a statistical test exists with an explicit, documented confidence level; and tests are tiered so CI can run the fast ones on every push.

That closes out Chapter 2's testing discipline. Chapter 3 turns to architecture — starting with the single decision that makes backend abstraction, multi-SDK support, and all of this chapter's construction tests possible in the first place: separating circuit logic from the backend it runs on.
